result:
There is a particular shade of grey that only exists at six in the morning, when the sky has decided to stay tentative but the streetlights have already surrendered. I have been thinking lately about thresholds—those invisible lines between one state and another. The moment a kettle stops screaming. The breath between someone finishing a sentence and you deciding whether to answer. The doorway of a library, where outside noise dies a little.

Libraries have a smell that I can almost taste: paper aging like bread, wood polish from years of hands, and occasionally the ghost of a coffee cup left too long. In them, silence is not empty; it is thick, inhabited by the turning of pages, the soft protest of a chair, the distant cough of a stranger who respects the covenant of quiet. I used to believe that stillness was the absence of sound, but now I think it is a presence all its own, a kind of music made of restraint.

Rain helps with this. It turns the world into a single, continuous sound, a white noise that makes everything feel temporarily solved. Watching it slide down glass, you realize how many thin boundaries we live behind—windows, eyelids, the membrane between thought and word. We are always in transition, even when we feel stuck.

I want to remember this: that before the day demands its shape, there is this small, unclaimed interval. That the kettle will boil, the rain will stop, the library will fill with footsteps, but for now, the grey is enough. There is no need to arrive at anything. The threshold is also a home.
